title: Manasseh: The Longest Reign and the Deepest Fall
summary: Hezekiah's son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years and undoes his father's reforms: he rebuilds the high places, builds altars to Baal and the stars inside the temple courts, sacrifices his son, consults mediums, and fills Jerusalem with innocent blood. Through the prophets the LORD announces that Jerusalem will be judged as Samaria was, wiped like a bowl and turned upside down. Manasseh's son Amon follows his ways for two years until he is assassinated, and the people of the land make the boy Josiah king.
story: Chapters 18 to 20 showed Judah at its best under Hezekiah, spared from Assyria because its king trusted the LORD. This chapter shows how quickly that could be lost. Manasseh is the Ahab of Judah, and the narrator makes the comparison explicit in verse 3. For the book of Kings, his reign is the point of no return: from here on, the fall of Jerusalem is announced as certain, and even Josiah's great reform in chapters 22 and 23 will not reverse it (23:26 and 24:3 name Manasseh's sins as the reason). The chapter explains to the book's first readers, living in or after the exile, why the city that survived Sennacherib did not survive Babylon.
historical:
Manasseh reigned from about 697 to 642 BC, probably including some years as co-regent with Hezekiah; his fifty-five years are the longest reign of any king of Israel or Judah. These were the decades when Assyria reached the peak of its power under Esarhaddon (681-669 BC) and Ashurbanipal (669 to about 631 BC), and Assyrian inscriptions name Manasseh of Judah among the western kings who sent tribute and supplied building materials for the Assyrian court. Judah survived as a loyal vassal. Some scholars suggest that Manasseh's religious policy reflects the pressures and fashions of that world, especially the worship of the heavenly bodies, which was prominent in Mesopotamia; others note that most of the practices listed were old Canaanite ones.

Second Chronicles 33 adds that Manasseh was taken captive to Babylon by the Assyrians, repented, and was restored, then removed foreign gods from the temple. Kings does not mention this, and historians debate how to relate the two accounts. A Jewish tradition preserved in later writings says the prophet Isaiah was killed under Manasseh, but that is not in the Bible. Amon reigned only about two years (about 642 to 640 BC). The people of the land who executed his killers were probably Judah's landowning citizens, who had also acted to secure the throne for the line of David after Athaliah (11:14-20).
cultural:
Almost every item in verses 3-7 is forbidden explicitly in Deuteronomy. The host of heaven means the sun, moon, and stars, worshiped as gods across the ancient Near East. Sorcery, divination, mediums, and spiritists (verse 6) were various ways of seeking hidden knowledge from spirits or the dead, all banned in Deuteronomy 18:10-12 as the practices of the nations. The carved Asherah pole (verse 7) was an image of the goddess Asherah, often associated in Canaanite religion with Baal and El. Setting it up in the temple, the house where the LORD had placed his Name, was the ultimate profanation.

The images of judgment in verse 13 come from building and household life. A measuring line and plumb line were used to check that a wall was straight; the LORD will measure Jerusalem by the same standard he used for Samaria and Ahab's house, with the same result. Wiping a bowl and turning it upside down was what you did after a meal to show it was finished and empty. Burial in a palace garden rather than in the royal tombs of the City of David (verses 18 and 26) may be a mark of dishonor, though the reason is not stated.
literary: The chapter is two regnal accounts of unequal length: Manasseh (verses 1-18) and Amon (verses 19-26). Manasseh's account is built as an indictment. Verses 2-9 list his sins, each one reversing something from Judah's past: what Hezekiah destroyed, he rebuilt; where the LORD placed his Name, he placed an idol. The narrator quotes the LORD's earlier promises about the temple (verses 4, 7-8) against the king who defiled it. Verses 10-15 then give the prophetic verdict in the form of a divine speech, and verse 16 adds a separate charge of bloodshed. The comparison with the Amorites and with Ahab, and the phrase "greater evil than the nations" (verse 9), make the point that Judah has become worse than the peoples it replaced. Amon's short account simply repeats his father's pattern.

doctrines.note: Manasseh brings idolatry into the temple itself, the place where the LORD had set his Name. The chapter shows idolatry not as a private preference but as a corruption of the whole of a nation's worship and life.
The measuring line and plumb line of verse 13 teach that God judges Jerusalem by the same standard as Samaria. Being the chosen city did not exempt Jerusalem; it made its sins weigh more.

Verse 9 says Manasseh led the people astray, and verse 16 adds innocent blood to idolatry. False worship and violence against the vulnerable go together, and a leader's sin spreads through a whole people.

words.note: Qav, a measuring line. Builders used it to lay out a straight wall. The prophets use it both for judgment and for restoration: Isaiah 28:17 speaks of justice as the measuring line, and Zechariah 1:16 promises that a line will be stretched out over a rebuilt Jerusalem. Here it measures the city for destruction.

Machah, to wipe or wipe out. The same verb is used in the flood story, when the LORD blots out living things from the earth (Genesis 7:23), and in 14:27, where he had not said he would blot out Israel's name. Now he says it of Jerusalem, using the homely image of wiping a dish clean.

Naqi, innocent, free of guilt. Innocent blood is the life of someone who did nothing to deserve death. The law treated its shedding as a pollution of the land that had to be answered (Deuteronomy 19:10; 21:8-9). Manasseh's filling Jerusalem with it is named again in 24:4 as a sin the LORD would not pardon.

christ: Kings presents Manasseh as a king of David's line who did the opposite of what that line was for, and his reign makes the fall of Jerusalem certain. The promise to David does not disappear, but it will have to be kept in a way beyond the kingdom Manasseh ruled. Manasseh's name appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10), a reminder that the Messiah's family line ran through its worst kings as well as its best. If Chronicles' account of Manasseh's repentance is read alongside Kings, his story also becomes a picture of grace reaching a man whose guilt was enormous, which the New Testament proclaims in Christ, whose own innocent blood was shed for the guilty. The link here is thematic: the chapter itself looks toward judgment, not rescue.

hard.q: If Manasseh repented, as 2 Chronicles says, why does Kings still blame him for Jerusalem's fall?
hard.a:
Kings never mentions Manasseh's repentance. Chronicles, written later and with different emphases, reports that he was captured, humbled himself, and was restored, and that he removed foreign gods from the temple. Some historians think Chronicles preserves a real episode that Kings omitted because it did not change the outcome; others think the Chronicler shaped the story to show a theme dear to him, that God responds to repentance in each generation. Readers who accept both accounts often note that Manasseh's personal repentance came late and did not undo the effect of decades of leadership on the nation, as Amon's reign shows.

The deeper question is why later generations suffered for Manasseh's sins. Kings does not claim that innocent people were punished for someone else's guilt. It says the people followed him (verse 9) and kept provoking the LORD from the exodus until this day (verse 15). Manasseh's reign is the decisive example of a long pattern, not the whole cause, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel, prophesying before the fall, insist that each generation was responsible for its own sins.

questions: Manasseh undid in a few years what his father had built. What practices in your own life or community protect what earlier faithfulness built?
The LORD said he would measure Jerusalem with the same line as Samaria. Where are you tempted to think that your privileges exempt you from the standards you apply to others?
Manasseh's sin led the whole people astray. How does the example of those in authority shape the faith of those under them, for good or ill?
